chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: The southwest tenor sound
summary: Love asks about the southwest tenor sound; Fields says all had a big tone and swing, naming Bert Jones, Hal Singer, Jacquet and Arnett Cobb.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: bus you had in Denver, it was a gorgeous little bus, blue.
Yeah, that might have been it, but later on--

Further on, there's always been the comments that the Texas and Oklahoma south-west bands had a distinctive or characteristic sound, especially the tenor players. Do you remember any of the guys like Bridges or John Hardy?
What was different about their sound?

One thing about it is, it's a funny thing, but it seemed like that all of them had a big tone; they didn't have this little tone and you talk about soul, it seemed like they were like Duke. You might read it soul but you might be calling it swing, and Duke said, don't mean a thing if it ain't got that swing.
And that's the way that they all seemed to play, one would have just a little of that touch. Did you ever know Bert Jones?
And there's this man that I got later on--
That's it, but he had it right in there. But the two guys, to tell you true that I consider the greatest that ever hailed from Texas was Jacquet and Arnett Cobb.
